blocks.text: Track every change made during one business transaction, then write them all to storage together or not at all.

A **unit of work** records objects that were created, modified or removed during one business transaction. Nothing hits storage until `commit()`, which writes every change in a valid order inside one transaction, each row once. It usually pairs with an **identity map**, so each row loads as one object, and finds changes by explicit registration or by comparing against load-time snapshots.

items: **Dirty detection:** caller calls `registerDirty`, or the UoW diffs snapshots (Hibernate).
**Commits:** one transaction: inserts, then updates, then deletes.

blocks.text: A unit of work is not thread-safe or long-lived. Share a repository, never a unit of work, across requests.

walkthrough.note: `load` is an identity map: one `Account` instance per id for the whole unit, plus a snapshot of the value as it was read.
New and removed objects must be registered, because no snapshot can reveal them. Modified objects need no call at all.
Dirty checking compares each loaded object with its snapshot. Writes go out in insert, update, delete order and are published in one swap, standing in for one transaction.
Two edits through two `load` calls hit the same object, so `a` is written once with its final value. `b` was read but unchanged, so it is not written.

blocks.text: Cancelling an order in a shop backend.

Cancelling must flip the order status, release reserved stock and credit the loyalty balance. Doing this with three independent saves leaves a half-cancelled order when the third fails. With a unit of work, the handler loads entities through it, mutates them as plain objects, and calls one `commit()`. With JPA, the persistence context plays that role: it detects the changes and flushes them in a single transaction.
Payoff: the three writes succeed or fail together, and each row is written at most once.

lists.title: Use when
items: Several entities change in one business operation and must succeed together.
You want to batch writes and write each changed entity once.
You need a single place for transaction boundaries.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Each request touches one row: a plain transactional `save` is enough.
Work spans services; a local transaction cannot cover it (see Saga).

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Long-lived units of work that hold stale objects and balloon in memory.
Sharing one across threads or requests.
Order of inserts and deletes violating foreign keys on flush.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Hand-writing change tracking when your ORM already provides it.
A custom unit of work wrapping a framework that already tracks changes.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Declarative `@Transactional` plus a JPA persistence context is a unit of work you rarely write by hand.
Try-with-resources on an `AutoCloseable` unit of work guarantees rollback when `commit()` is not reached.

rows.difference: Repositories read and register aggregates; the unit of work decides when those changes are written, and in what order.
The unit of work chooses what to write and when; mappers perform the actual row translation for each change.
Active Record saves each object immediately on `save()`, so there is no shared transaction scope or batching unless you add one.
A unit of work is one local transaction in one store. A saga coordinates several transactions across services with compensations.
Events raised by entities during the unit of work are usually dispatched after a successful commit.

exercises.prompt: Explain Unit of Work in your own words: what does it track, when does it write, and what is it not?

modelAnswer.text: A unit of work records new, changed and removed objects during one business transaction and writes them together at commit, in a valid order, in one transaction. With an identity map it loads each row once and can detect changes by diffing snapshots. It is request-scoped and local to one store, so it is not a saga.

keyPoints: Tracks new, dirty and removed objects
Identity map: one object per row
Local to one store; a saga spans services
